title: An L³ bound for the dyadic triangular Hilbert form
coverage: I read the whole paper (Sections 1–5, about 750 lines of LaTeX) and checked each step by hand. Sec 2: the Daletskii–Krein Hessian b_P, with the factor 3/2 checked; the order comparison via operator monotonicity of sqrt and L_B, including the a>=1 semidefinite limit; the midpoint gap constant 1/(2√2), from T+tU<=2T. Sec 3: A_v=MP_vM matches T_v up to block permutation; the bound E>=Q/2, from b_{M^2}(MDM)=(3/2)Q and the 1/3 loss on a sum of three terms; Q>=A/2+E, using 2q_i/(q_i+q_j)>=1; the cubic case split into 3E_i, 3sqrt(A_iE_i) and A_i (the sqrt(q_i) factors check out); A+3E+3sqrt(AE)<=5(A/2+E); tr((DM)^3)=6τ, using transposes for the reverse orientation; and the final 5/3. Sec 4: the weight normalization gives L=2^{2k}τ; the child edge matrix is C W C, with C=sqrt(2)×projection and doubled weights; the child row-star Gram has no cross term, so pairwise independence of the signs gives E[RR*|s_v]=C R R* C; then Jensen, the Gram swap Φ(CRR*C)=Φ(T+sU), and the final constant 10√2/3. Sec 5: tr T^{3/2}<=(tr T)^{3/2} and the power-mean bound √2(a^3+b^3); each edge counted twice, giving 2√2; the bijection between pairs and triples via XOR; telescoping via the unique admissible parent and 2^{2k}/4=2^{2(k-1)}; the constant (10√2/3)(2√2)·3=40; the one-scale Hölder bound giving ℓ1 continuity; and the density argument. I also ran a numerical test: 3000 random step-function configurations of mixed sizes gave δ>=0 and max |τ|/δ ≈ 0.22, against the claimed bound 4.71.
main_claim: For every finite S⊂Z and every real input in L^3(R_+^2), the sum over k in S and over admissible XOR triples of |L_I(F0,F1,F2)| is at most 40‖F0‖_3‖F1‖_3‖F2‖_3. The proof uses a Bellman/energy telescoping with the energy tr((R*R)^{3/2}) of the row stars and a mixed trace estimate with constant 5/3.
sibling_notes: The sibling paper (rank 434, annular variation, same family) cites the same companion OpenAI2026 mixed trace estimate and also got no_gap_found. This paper reproves everything it needs from the companion (Sections 2–3), so it does not depend on it circularly.
